What Is Express?

A minimal HTTP framework, and the request/response cycle it's built around.

Laravel is a batteries-included framework: routing, an ORM, validation, auth scaffolding, a templating engine, and much more, all ship together and are wired up for you. Express is deliberately not that. It's a small library that gives you exactly two things: a way to define routes, and a way to run functions (middleware) in between a request arriving and a response going out. Everything else — the ORM (Prisma, from Week 2), validation (Zod, Week 3), auth (Week 4) — gets added as separate packages, on purpose, rather than bundled in.

That trade-off is deliberate on Express's part: you assemble only what you need, at the cost of more upfront wiring than Laravel gives you for free. This course does that wiring explicitly, week by week, so you see what a framework like Laravel is normally doing for you behind the scenes.

Figure 1.3 is the entire Express setup for this API so far.

// Figure 1.3: the whole Express app (src/app.js)
import express from 'express';
import routes from './routes/index.js';
import notFound from './middleware/notFound.js';
import errorHandler from './middleware/errorHandler.js';

const app = express();

app.use(express.json());

app.use(routes);

app.use(notFound);
app.use(errorHandler);

export default app;

express() creates the application object. Every other line either registers something to run on incoming requests (app.use(...)) or exports the finished app so something else (server.js) can start listening on it. That's the whole request/response cycle at this level: a request comes in, it passes through whatever's registered via app.use, in order, until something sends a response.

Notice app.js builds all of that but never actually starts the server — there's no app.listen(...) anywhere in it. That split is deliberate enough to deserve its own explanation, next.
